tldr: In simulation benchmarks where state-of-the-art VLA models boast high success rates, a simple training-free kNN retrieval-based approach reaches a 91.7% success rate, matching or even outperforming many trained VLAs—a striking result that challenges our understanding of VLA generalization.
hero_caption: Overview of the evaluation pipeline in this study. (a) A training-free kNN method that retrieves the closest demonstrations to the current observation and outputs a weighted average of their action chunks, compared under identical conditions against (b) a standard VLA policy that directly predicts actions using a large VLM backbone and an action head.
overview:
In recent robot learning research, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—which combine vision-language models (VLMs) with action generation heads—have taken center stage. On the standard simulation benchmark LIBERO, modern VLAs achieve success rates exceeding 95%, making it seem as though robotic manipulation has achieved strong generalization. However, other studies report that minor changes to camera viewpoints or initial robot poses cause performance to plummet. This raises a fundamental question: are these stellar benchmark scores truly proof of generalization to unseen situations, or are the models merely memorizing and replaying demonstration trajectories?

To investigate, the authors built a simple k-nearest neighbors (kNN) policy that requires no policy training at all. It simply retrieves the demonstration states most similar to the current observation and reuses their subsequent action chunks (sequences of consecutive actions). Remarkably, a multimodal kNN using standard ResNet-18 and CLIP features achieved an outstanding 91.7% success rate on LIBERO. Furthermore, under the perturbed LIBERO-Plus benchmark, it outperformed seven of the nine publicly available VLAs evaluated and showed the smallest performance drop among all tested policies, highlighting its strong robustness.

In addition, the authors thoroughly dissected nine public VLAs. They discovered that fine-tuning primarily transforms the VLM backbone into a "better retrieval key" and that the actions output by VLAs remain extremely close to the training demonstrations. These findings reveal that much of the high performance exhibited by VLAs on current benchmarks can be explained by the local retrieval and reuse of demonstration data.
contributions: Demonstrated that a simple, training-free kNN retrieval-based method achieves a 91.7% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark and exhibits the smallest performance drop under perturbed environments (LIBERO-Plus).
Evaluated nine publicly available VLA backbones as retrieval keys, revealing that the primary effect of fine-tuning is transforming the backbone into a more robust retrieval key.

Showed that the action chunks output by VLAs correlate very strongly with training demonstrations and kNN predictions ($R^2$ up to 0.93), illustrating that their practical behavior closely mimics demonstration replay.
Introduced Local Action Consistency (LAC), a novel offline metric that measures the quality of a retrieval representation without requiring policy rollouts in the environment or simulator.

sections.heading: Are High Benchmark Scores Truly Generalization, or Just Demo Retrieval?
sections.summary: While state-of-the-art VLA models achieve over 95% success on LIBERO, they are known to be fragile under environmental perturbations. Using a training-free kNN retrieval policy as a baseline and diagnostic tool, this work asks how much of current VLA performance can be explained by simple retrieval and reuse of demonstrations.
sections.details:
In modern robotics research, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—which attach action heads such as diffusion models or flow matching to large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)—have become standard. On LIBERO, a standard robot simulation benchmark, modern VLAs achieve success rates around 97%, nearing benchmark saturation.

However, recent studies (such as LIBERO-Plus) show that minor perturbations to camera views, initial robot positions, language instructions, visual appearance, or object placements cause sharp drops in success rates for these high-performing VLAs. This leads to an important question: does success on the benchmark truly reflect generalization to unseen environments, or is it merely memorization of demonstration trajectories?

To address this question directly, the authors proposed an entirely training-free action retrieval approach using k-nearest neighbors (kNN). The method simply retrieves demonstration frames nearest to the current observation, combines their subsequent action chunks, and executes them. Through this approach, the study rigorously quantifies what fraction of benchmark performance can be explained purely by retrieval, and how heavily the internal representations and output actions of existing public VLAs rely on demonstrations.

captions.F1: The comparative framework of this work. In (a), observation embeddings are used to retrieve demonstration embeddings and output a weighted average of action chunks, whereas in (b), a VLA predicts actions directly through neural networks. Both are evaluated fairly under the exact same rollout environment and protocol.

sections.heading: Retrieval in Robot Learning and the VLA Generalization vs. Memorization Debate
sections.summary: Retrieval methods in robot learning have traditionally been used for data curation and context provision, but non-parametric controllers are also remarkably strong. This work presents a training-free retrieval approach using pretrained representations, complementing studies that analyze how VLA fine-tuning affects representations and generalization.
sections.details:
### Retrieval in Robot Learning
Historically, retrieval in robotics has primarily been used to select trajectories from offline datasets (e.g., Behavior Retrieval, FlowRetrieval) or to supply in-context examples for VLAs (e.g., REGENT, RICL). Meanwhile, other approaches use retrieval directly as a control policy, such as VINN performing nearest-neighbor regression in a learned visual feature space, or studies showing that diffusion policy actions stay close to the training data. The key distinction of this work is that it requires no policy training whatsoever, using a standard ResNet-18 or frozen backbones from existing VLAs directly as retrieval keys.

### VLA Generalization and Memorization
Even when VLAs achieve over 95% success on LIBERO, their performance drops drastically under the perturbations introduced by LIBERO-Plus. Furthermore, studies have reported that models often blindly execute memorized motion patterns even when instructions or objects change (LIBERO-PRO), and that supervised fine-tuning can overwrite useful semantic features originally present in VLMs. This study digs deeper into the reality of VLA memorization and generalization by directly measuring how fine-tuning alters the quality of backbones as retrieval keys.

sections.heading: Control Without Training: The Multimodal kNN Policy and the LAC Metric
sections.summary: From a memory bank storing observations and action chunks, nearest-neighbor demonstrations are retrieved using a multimodal weighted distance, and actions are output via a softmax-weighted average. The authors also introduce LAC, an offline metric to evaluate representation quality for retrieval without running the simulator.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Memory Construction
A retrieval memory bank is built from offline demonstration trajectories. From 1,693 demonstrations in LIBERO, every second frame stores the observation image $o_i$, the subsequent action chunk of horizon $H$ steps, and the trajectory index. This yields a memory space of approximately 137k entries.

### 3.2 Retrieval Distance Computation
The distance $d(q, i)$ between a current query observation $q$ and memory entry $i$ is defined as a multimodal weighted distance combining vision, robot proprioception, language instructions, elapsed episode time, and recent observation history. Each modality's distance is normalized by scaling with the intra-task median distance to balance differences across physical units.

### 3.3 Neighbor Selection and Action Prediction
The top-$k$ nearest candidates are selected, but with a specific constraint: to prevent over-reliance on any single demonstration trajectory, at most one entry is allowed per demonstration trajectory. Softmax weights $\alpha_i$ are computed from the retrieval distances for the chosen $k$ action chunks, and their linear combination produces the final predicted action chunk.

### 3.4 Offline Metric: Local Action Consistency (LAC)
LAC quantifies the intuition that in a good representation space, states that are close together should also share similar future actions. For an evaluated query, relative to the action differences across all entries within the same task, it scores how similar the action chunks of the $k$ nearest neighbors in representation space are. This enables practitioners to evaluate whether a representation is well-suited for retrieval-based control without running rollouts in simulation.

sections.heading: Experimental Protocol and kNN Policy Implementations
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across LIBERO's 4 suites (40 tasks, 2,000 episodes) and LIBERO-Plus with 7 types of perturbations (420 variants). Three kNN policy variants—ResNet-only, multimodal, and LAC-optimized keys—were benchmarked against nine public VLAs.
sections.details:
### Evaluation Benchmark and Public VLAs
Evaluations used all 40 tasks across the four LIBERO suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long), running 50 episodes per task for a total of 2,000 rollouts following the official protocol. Robustness was evaluated using LIBERO-Plus, which features 420 perturbed test settings covering lighting, camera viewpoints, and object colors. For comparison, nine publicly available VLA checkpoints from LeRobot were evaluated with their default inference settings: $\pi_0$, $\pi_0$-FAST, $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, VLA-JEPA, Evo-1, X-VLA, MolmoAct2, and GR00T N1.7.

### Three kNN Policy Variants
- **k-NN (ResNet)**: Uses only image features from the 3rd layer ($4\times 4$ feature grid) of a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18. It searches only within demonstrations of the specified task and executes the weighted average chunk of $k=8$ neighbors.
- **k-NN (multimodal)**: Searches across demonstrations of all tasks. It combines visual features, robot state, CLIP language embeddings, elapsed time, and observation history, setting $k=13$. It also applies mode seeking (downweighting candidates deviating from the dominant action mode) and temporal ensembling (re-planning and blending overlapping chunks at each step).
- **k-NN (LAC key)**: Based on the multimodal setup, this applies a linear projection layer trained on ResNet features using a differentiable surrogate of the LAC loss.

### Repurposing VLA Backbones as Retrieval Keys
To examine the representational quality of VLAs themselves, experiments were also conducted where pooled intermediate image token hidden states from each VLA's VLM were used directly as retrieval keys instead of ResNet.

sections.heading: Surprising Results: kNN Rivals VLAs, and VLA Actions Mirror Demonstrations
sections.summary: Multimodal kNN scored 91.7% on LIBERO and 82.4% on LIBERO-Plus, outperforming many trained VLAs. Furthermore, fine-tuning VLAs primarily turns their backbones into superior retrieval keys, and the actions output by VLAs match weighted averages of demonstration trajectories with remarkable fidelity.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Benchmark Results: Over 90% Success via Pure Retrieval
k-NN (multimodal) achieved a 91.7% success rate on standard LIBERO and 82.4% on LIBERO-Plus. This matches $\pi_0$-FAST and clearly outperforms SmolVLA and the original $\pi_0$. Its robustness under perturbations is especially striking: while VLA-JEPA, Evo-1, and X-VLA exceeded 94% on standard LIBERO, their performance collapsed significantly on LIBERO-Plus. In contrast, k-NN (multimodal) dropped by only 9.3 percentage points—the smallest decrease among all evaluated policies—outperforming 7 of the 9 VLAs under perturbations.

### 6.2 Ablation Study: What Matters Most?
Ablation analysis revealed that the most critical components are visual representations ($-34.5$ points when falling back to raw pixels), language prompts ($-27.1$ points when excluded), and demonstration volume ($-14.3$ points when reduced to 10%). On the other hand, temporal ensembling, history matching, and proprioceptive robot state each contributed less than 1 percentage point, demonstrating that basic nearest-neighbor retrieval over multimodal representations is what fundamentally drives performance.

### 6.3 Representation Analysis: What Does Fine-Tuning Actually Do?
When using VLA backbones directly as retrieval keys, fine-tuning improved retrieval success rates on LIBERO-Plus for 7 out of 8 models (improvements ranging from 5 to 37 points). As visualized with t-SNE, the representation space before fine-tuning was partitioned by scene suites, whereas after fine-tuning it formed smooth trajectories aligned with episode progress (Figure F3). In some models, retrieving demo actions via kNN directly from the backbone yielded up to a 48-point higher success rate than passing through their trained action heads.

### 6.4 Action Space Analysis: VLA Actions Mirror the Demos
Comparing the action chunks generated by VLAs during rollouts against the action chunks predicted by kNN from demonstrations revealed exceptionally high coefficients of determination ($R^2$ between 0.63 and 0.93). In 5 out of 8 models, the VLA's actions were actually closer to the kNN retrieval predictions than to the unseen test ground-truth demonstrations. This strongly suggests that modern VLAs are largely reproducing and interpolating demonstration trajectories.

### 6.5 LAC as an Offline Diagnostic
The proposed LAC metric exhibited a strong correlation ($r = 0.78$) with closed-loop rollout success rates in the environment. Moreover, simply training a linear projection on ResNet features to optimize LAC boosted kNN success rates from 88.7% to 93.0%.

captions.F3: t-SNE visualization of retrieval keys for 4,150 LIBERO demonstration frames. The top row shows representations before fine-tuning, and the bottom row shows them after fine-tuning (or after LAC training), colored by episode progress. Fine-tuning aligns representations into smooth trajectories along task progress and narrows progress gaps between demonstrations (the far-right $\pi_0$ is an outlier where representations collapsed per task).

sections.heading: Are We Merely "Retrieving" Demonstrations?
sections.summary: This work shows that in benchmarks with dense demonstrations, kNN retrieval alone rivals full VLA performance. Future VLA research should routinely include retrieval baselines like kNN to distinguish true generalization from demonstration memorization and replay.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that on standard benchmarks with dense demonstrations like LIBERO, matching states and reusing demonstration actions can solve the vast majority of tasks without any complex policy training. Moreover, fine-tuning primarily refines VLA backbones into "better retrieval keys," with action heads often outputting actions that closely mirror retrieved demonstrations.

Of course, these findings do not imply that kNN is a universal solution for all robotic manipulation. By design, kNN cannot extrapolate to entirely novel trajectories absent from memory. However, this also strongly implies that much of what is currently celebrated as "VLA generalization" may simply be sophisticated nearest-neighbor interpolation enabled by dense benchmark coverage. Moving forward, properly assessing true generalization will require reporting retrieval baselines, evaluating on sparsely demonstrated regimes, and testing setups with truly unseen object configurations.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Parameters, Full Task Results, and Perturbation Breakdowns
sections.summary: This appendix details distance normalization formulas, hyperparameter optimization findings, complete results across all 40 tasks and perturbation categories, and PCA analyses showing structural shifts in representation space.
sections.details:
### Hyperparameter Sensitivity
Optimization via Optuna revealed that the number of neighbors $k$ (57% relative importance) and the constraint of selecting at most one entry per demonstration trajectory (25% importance) were the most critical factors. Removing the trajectory constraint makes the policy prone to failure by overfitting to local idiosyncrasies of a single demonstration.

### Performance by Task and Perturbation Category
As shown in Figure F6, across all 40 tasks in both standard LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, multimodal kNN (orange labels) consistently maintained performance competitive with top VLAs. In the perturbation breakdown (Figure F7), while all policies showed resilience to lighting changes, camera viewpoint shifts caused substantial degradation across the board. Notably, k-NN (LAC key) retained an 88% success rate under viewpoint shifts, vastly outperforming other policies (which maxed out at 73%).

### Untangling Representations via PCA
Prior to fine-tuning, 40% to 84% of the variance in the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) of VLM representations was explained by differences between suites (scene environments; Figure F9). After fine-tuning, this fraction dropped dramatically to between 1% and 43%, confirming that background scene variance is suppressed in favor of features directly aligned with manipulation actions.

captions.F6: Heatmap of policy success rates across all 40 tasks in LIBERO (top) and LIBERO-Plus (bottom). Tasks are ordered by average difficulty, visually illustrating that kNN variants (orange text) achieve performance competitive with, or even more consistent than, state-of-the-art VLAs.
captions.F9: Plots of the first and second principal components (PC1 and PC2) for each retrieval key, colored by LIBERO suite (scene). Before fine-tuning, representations cleanly separate by suite (reflecting background dependence), whereas after fine-tuning they blend together, drastically reducing the proportion of scene-dependent variance.

takeaways: In environments with dense demonstrations like LIBERO, a training-free multimodal kNN retrieval approach achieves a 91.7% success rate.

High benchmark scores in modern VLAs are likely driven not by broad generalization to novel situations, but by VLM backbones acting as high-capacity retrieval keys that replay actions close to demonstrations.
For several VLAs, directly retrieving demonstration actions from backbone features via kNN yields higher success rates and better perturbation robustness than using their trained action heads.
Future VLA research should include training-free kNN retrieval baselines alongside benchmark scores to accurately evaluate true generalization performance.
limitations: Conclusions are based on a simulation benchmark (LIBERO) with dense demonstration coverage; results may not directly extrapolate to real-world tasks requiring novel trajectory synthesis or operating in demonstration-sparse settings.

Perturbations in LIBERO-Plus primarily involve shifts in visual appearance and initial poses, without testing scenarios where robots must search for or generate fundamentally new motion paths from scratch.

Some public VLA checkpoints evaluated scored below their reported peak performance in original papers, reflecting slight limits in reproduction fidelity for specific model weights and implementations.
